questions.q: How does Salesforce's own architecture guidance describe "Large Data Volumes"?
options: A deliberately elastic, imprecise term oriented around tens of millions of records or hundreds of GB of storage, not a fixed threshold
Exactly 1 million records in any single object
Any org with more than 100 active users
A fixed Salesforce Support classification that must be requested before it applies
questions.explain: Salesforce describes LDV as elastic and imprecise, giving tens of thousands of users, tens of millions of records, or hundreds of GB as a rough reference point rather than a hard number.

questions.q: Why can LDV problems pass undetected in a sandbox with a few thousand seed records?
options: Sandboxes disable all indexing by default
Sandbox data is always encrypted differently than production data
The specific behaviors that cause LDV problems, like index selectivity thresholds and data skew, are a function of record count, so they don't appear until real production volume exists
LDV only affects custom objects, which sandboxes don't include
questions.explain: Selectivity thresholds, data skew, and sharing-recalculation cost are all volume-dependent, so logic that is perfectly correct looks fine at low record counts and only breaks once a much larger production volume is reached.

questions.q: A nightly batch job against a 4-million-record object starts timing out due to record locks during updates. Which LDV symptom category does this fall into?
options: Volume-management symptom
Write-path symptom
Read-path symptom
This isn't an LDV symptom at all, since batch jobs are unrelated to data volume
questions.explain: Record locking during updates is a write-path problem — it affects data loads and bulk updates, which this course covers in Chapter 2.

questions.q: Which of the following is a volume-management symptom, as this course categorizes it?
options: A SOQL query that used to return instantly now needs an index to stay fast
A batch update intermittently fails because of record locks on a shared parent
A role hierarchy change takes an unexpectedly long time to recalculate sharing
An org has accumulated years of inactive records that make every other LDV problem worse over time unless something actively manages it
questions.explain: Volume-management symptoms are about the org simply carrying more data than it needs to keep active, which is a distinct category from the read-path (query slowdowns) and write-path (locking, skew, sharing recalculation) symptoms covered elsewhere.

questions.q: Why does this course treat Large Data Volumes as its own architectural discipline, rather than folding it into general data-modeling best practices?
options: Because the failure modes that define LDV only become visible at a scale most projects don't reach until well after go-live, so they need dedicated attention rather than being assumed to be caught by normal data-modeling review
Because LDV only applies to orgs using Big Objects
Because Salesforce requires a separate certification exam for LDV specifically
Because LDV has nothing to do with data modeling at all
questions.explain: LDV problems are late-arriving by nature — they depend on record count, not on whether the underlying logic or data model is otherwise correct — which is exactly why they warrant dedicated architectural attention rather than being assumed away by general design review.
